result.reason: Both items present the core mishnah text introducing the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Chachamim about whether the seller must purchase access rights to the retained well — exactly what heading 4 ('Seller Retains Well') describes as its topic, framing this as 'a debate between Rabbi Akiva and the Chachamim.'

The passage describes the case where the seller sells the pit/cistern to another while retaining the house, with Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis debating whether the buyer needs to purchase access rights — which matches exactly the prose under 'Seller Sells Well.'

This Gemara passage discusses the distinction between bor and dut, which is part of the Gemara's analysis following the mishnah — it fits under 'Generous vs. Stingy Sale' where the prose describes the Gemara attempting to characterize the debate more precisely and examining the textual foundations, rather than under 'Generous Seller Principle' which discusses the abstract principle itself.

Both items present the Gemara's initial framing of the Rabbi Akiva vs. Chachamim debate as mocher be-ayin yafah vs. be-ayin ra'ah, and note that this mishnah is the source for Rabbi Akiva's general principle — exactly what the 'Generous vs. Stingy Sale' prose describes.

The passage presents the Gemara's challenge that the dispute may be specific to this case rather than a general principle, explaining Rabbi Akiva's concern for the buyer's privacy (not wanting others to tread on his property) — which directly matches the 'Privacy Protection Theory' prose discussing the psychology of the buyer and Rabbi Akiva's sensitivity to the buyer's situation.

The passage presents the seifa proof showing that Rabbi Akiva and the Chachamim's positions reverse when the seller sells the pit to another, which is precisely what the 'Positions Reverse' section's prose describes as the Gemara's dismantling of local readings by pointing to the seifa.

The passage discusses whether Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis disagree about following the buyer's vs. seller's intent, which is the abstract principle ('batar da'ata de-lokei'ach' vs. 'batar da'ata de-mocher') that the 'Field Sale Flip' prose explicitly establishes as the conclusion of the fourfold repetition.

Candidate 3's prose explicitly describes the moker le-acher field case (items 5-6), the shema mina conclusion establishing the general principle, and the Rav/Shmuel halakhic dispute (items 7-8), while also covering the preliminary why-repeat discussion (items 1-4) in its broader narrative.

Both items together introduce Ravina's question about whether Rav and Shmuel follow their general reasoning, and then cite Rav Naḥman quoting Shmuel about brothers who divided — this is exactly the content described in candidate 0's prose ('The Gemara introduces a parallel dispute... Rav Nachman amar Shmuel: when brothers divide an inherited estate'), not the enumeration of consequences described in candidate 1.

The passage contains both Rav Naḥman's warning ('be careful with these, they are established halakhot') and Rav's position ('yesh lahem'), which together form the conclusion of the 'No Cross-Rights' section as described in its prose, which explicitly quotes both 've-zaharu ba-hem halachot kevuot hem' and mentions Rav's 'yesh lahem' response.
Both items together form the classic Talmudic 'tzerikha' argument explaining why both cases must be stated independently, which is precisely what the 'Why Both Cases Needed' prose section describes.

The passage records Rav Naḥman asking Rav Huna whose opinion the halacha follows and Rav Huna answering 'yours' (Shmuel's camp), which is precisely what heading 0 'Follow Shmuel' describes — the question of which camp's ruling prevails and the answer that halacha follows Shmuel.

The passage covers all three sub-cases (both sold, both gifts, outer gift/inner sale) in a single Talmudic statement, making it most naturally placed under the 'Physical Setup' heading that introduces the general scenario, rather than splitting it under one of the specific sub-case headings.

Both items together present the case of outer-by-sale/inner-by-gift: item 1 gives the initial (mistaken) understanding that no access rights exist, and item 2 refutes it with the 'generous eye' principle — exactly the scenario and ruling described in the 'Gift Gets Access' prose.
